title: Lipid Transport & Lipoproteins
objectives: Describe the structure and function of major lipoprotein classes
Trace the exogenous and endogenous lipid transport pathways
Explain cholesterol metabolism and reverse cholesterol transport
Diagnose and manage dyslipidemias and their clinical consequences

overview.title: Lipoprotein Overview
overview.content:
Lipoprotein Structure

  • Composition: Neutral lipid core (TG/cholesteryl esters) + amphipathic shell (phospholipids, free cholesterol, apolipoproteins)
  • Key apolipoproteins: ApoB-48 (chylomicrons), ApoB-100 (VLDL/LDL), ApoA-I (HDL)
  • Density classes: Chylomicrons < VLDL < IDL < LDL < HDL

exogenous_pathway.title: Exogenous Pathway
exogenous_pathway.content:
Dietary Fat Transport

1. Chylomicron Formation

  • Intestinal enterocytes package dietary TGs + cholesterol into chylomicrons (ApoB-48)
  • Requires: MTP (microsomal triglyceride transfer protein)

2. Circulation & Lipolysis

  • LPL (lipoprotein lipase) hydrolyzes TGs → FFA for tissues (ApoC-II activates LPL)
  • Chylomicron remnants delivered to liver via ApoE recognition
  • Deficiency: LPL/ApoC-II deficiency → Type I hyperlipidemia

endogenous_pathway.title: Endogenous Pathway
endogenous_pathway.content:
Hepatic Lipid Transport

1. VLDL Secretion

  • Liver packages hepatic TGs into VLDL (ApoB-100)
  • Regulation: Insulin inhibits VLDL production

2. LDL Formation

  • VLDL → IDL (via LPL) → LDL (via hepatic lipase)
  • Fate: LDL delivers cholesterol to peripheral tissues via LDL receptor (ApoB-100 recognition)
  • Hypercholesterolemia: LDL receptor defects → Type IIa

reverse_transport.title: Reverse Cholesterol Transport
reverse_transport.content:
HDL Metabolism

1. HDL Biogenesis

  • Nascent HDL forms from liver/intestine (ApoA-I + phospholipids)
  • ABC1 transporter loads free cholesterol from tissues

2. Cholesterol Esterification

  • LCAT (lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase) converts FC → CE (ApoA-I activates)
  • Mature HDL delivers CE to liver (SR-B1 receptor) or transfers to LDL (CETP)
  • Target: CETP inhibitors raise HDL

disorders.title: Clinical Disorders
disorders.content:
Dyslipidemias

1. Primary Dyslipidemias

  • Type I: LPL deficiency → milky plasma (↑↑ chylomicrons)
  • Type IIa: LDL receptor defect → ↑LDL (xanthomas, CAD)
  • Type III: ApoE2 homozygosity → ↑β-VLDL (palmar xanthomas)

2. Atherosclerosis

  • Pathogenesis: Oxidized LDL uptake by macrophages → foam cells → plaque
  • Risk factors: High LDL, low HDL, smoking, hypertension

3. Treatment

  • Statins: HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors (↑LDL receptors)
  • Ezetimibe: Blocks NPC1L1 (intestinal cholesterol absorption)
  • PCSK9 inhibitors: Prevent LDL receptor degradation

faqs.title: FAQs
faqs.content:
FAQs

Q: Why does HDL have cardioprotective effects? +

A: HDL removes arterial cholesterol (reverse transport), has anti-inflammatory/antioxidant properties, and inhibits LDL oxidation.

Q: How do statins reduce cardiovascular risk beyond LDL lowering? +

A: Pleiotropic effects include improved endothelial function, plaque stabilization, and reduced inflammation via isoprenoid inhibition.

Q: Why are chylomicrons absent in fasting plasma? +

A: Chylomicron half-life is 5-15 minutes; they're rapidly cleared after meals. Persistent chylomicronemia suggests LPL deficiency.
